lesson.title: The Baby Boom: A Generation Born into Postwar Prosperity
lesson.summary: Between roughly 1946 and 1964, the United States experienced a sustained surge in births driven by the economic security that followed World War II, producing a generation large enough to reshape American schools, suburbs, and consumer culture for decades.
lesson.body:
The Great Depression of the 1930s had pushed many Americans to delay marriage and childbearing, and the years of World War II, when millions of men served overseas and the economy was organized entirely around war production, delayed things further still. That pent up demand for ordinary family life, combined with genuine postwar optimism, helps explain what happened once the war ended in 1945: birth rates in the United States rose sharply and stayed high for nearly two decades, a period historians call the baby boom, generally dated from about 1946 to 1964. Roughly 76 million children were born in the United States during those years, making the baby boomer generation one of the largest in the nation's history.

Several forces converged to make this possible. Wartime production had pulled the country out of Depression era unemployment and left American industry, largely undamaged by the fighting itself, ready to shift toward building homes, cars, and appliances instead of tanks and planes. The Servicemen's Readjustment Act of 1944, better known as the GI Bill, gave millions of returning veterans low cost home loans and funded college education, making homeownership and a stable career newly reachable for a huge share of American families. Its benefits reached white veterans far more fully than Black veterans, since local banks and universities often administered the program in ways that shut Black applicants out in practice even though the law itself did not exclude them by name.

That new prosperity built new places to live. Developers such as the Levitt family used mass production techniques, borrowed in part from wartime manufacturing, to build entire suburban communities quickly and affordably. Levittown, built on Long Island, New York, starting in 1947, became the best known example and a symbol of the era's suburban expansion, followed soon after by similar developments across the country. These new suburbs grew up around the young families of the baby boom, complete with new schools, shopping centers, and, before long, the interstate highways that connected them to nearby cities.

The scale of the baby boom left a lasting mark on American institutions. School districts scrambled to build enough classrooms and hire enough teachers throughout the 1950s and into the 1960s. Toy, appliance, and children's clothing industries expanded rapidly to meet demand. And because this generation was so large, its members would go on to shape American politics, culture, and the economy at every stage of their lives, from the crowded schools of the 1950s to the workplaces and voting patterns of later decades.
